title: Leaders Are Great Students of Cause and Effect
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that identifying symptoms is not the same as understanding root cause, and that good leaders resist the temptation to settle on the first plausible explanation for a problem. It introduces the 'fish diagram' (fishbone diagram) technique as a structured way to brainstorm and test multiple possible causes before concluding on one, and stresses validating theories with trusted colleagues rather than relying on a single leader's judgment. The piece frames this discipline of asking 'why' as a defining habit of effective leadership.
points: Leaders should resist settling on the first plausible cause of a problem and instead generate and test multiple competing explanations.
The fishbone diagram technique structures root-cause brainstorming by mapping possible contributing factors as 'bones' branching off the core problem.
Validating a suspected cause by defending it to other smart, informed colleagues catches faulty assumptions before they drive a decision.
Good leaders treat cause and effect as two sides of the same reality and make asking 'why' a habitual practice, not a one-off exercise.
quotes: For leaders, it's not enough to see patterns and to recognize what is happening. Leaders are expected to know why.
The key is to avoid presuming a cause without validating it with others.
In the so-called Fish Diagram method, a leader writes the problem or effect on the far-right side of a piece of paper, flip chart, or whiteboard.
Now, take a step back and discuss the many possibilities with one or more trusted colleagues.
They recognize that cause and effect are two sides of the same reality. Their job is to deal expertly with both sides.
